title: Base-2 digits of powers of 3 look random beyond small-scale structure

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Base-2 digits of powers of 3 look random beyond small-scale structure

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Successive powers of 3 written in base 2 form a pattern that, apart from some small-scale structure, appears random for all practical purposes, even though it comes from repeated multiplication by 3.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Some small-scale structure is visible, but on a larger scale the pattern seems for all practical purposes random.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 4, “Systems Based on Numbers”; section “Elementary Arithmetic” (from p. 117), p. 120. Scope: base-2 digit sequences of powers of 3

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch04-03: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.81

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Arbitrarily many exact digits can be generated cheaply and tested with public standard software. The phrase for all practical purposes is test-relative, so existing computation strongly resolves operationalized versions but not an unrestricted randomness assertion.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Generate binary expansions of 3^n over large preregistered ranges and test digit frequencies, runs, correlations, compressibility, and two-dimensional pattern statistics against matched random sequences. Significant persistent deviations refute practical randomness under those tests; passing supports but cannot prove it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The two-dimensional arrangement across powers admits many analysis choices.

Passing finite statistical tests cannot establish randomness.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.65
operationalizability: 0.7
data adequacy: 0.75
analysis feasibility: 0.98
data existence: 0.98

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The object is a single explicit sequence, and 'for all practical purposes' matches a large finite computation rather than an unproved normality theorem. Arbitrary-precision powers of 3 are immediate to generate, and either a clear large-scale pattern or its continued absence decides the practical claim. The open number-theoretic question of normality is a stronger statement than the one Wolfram makes.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compute a very long prefix of the base-2 digits of successive powers of 3, remove the small-scale triangular structure, and run equidistribution, autocorrelation, and compression tests. A stable large-scale regularity refutes 'random for all practical purposes'; its absence on prefixes far beyond practical use confirms the claim as stated.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The acknowledged small-scale structure has to be excluded by a declared filter, or it will be counted as a regularity.

Tests on a finite prefix cannot prove that the infinite digit array is normal or pattern-free.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.95
analysis feasibility: 0.9
operationalizability: 0.72
data adequacy: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.6
